catalog_quote: 5.4.2 Stress. Stress occurs on the last syllable of a word if the same pitch is on all syllables. In a word with various pitches, stress occurs on the highest pitch. In a word with two pitches of the same height which are the highest in the word, stress occurs on the syllable closest to the end of the word. [p. 86] ... 5. SUPRASEGMENTALS. There are two level pitches in Obokuitai, represented by /1/ (high) and /2/ (low). The downglide /12/ symbolizes a falling pitch. [p. 81] ... In the following examples, pitches [1'] and [12'] represent slightly higher pitches than [1] and [12]. Syllables with the single vowel /i/ possess this higher pitch. [p. 82] ... 4.1 The Syllable. The syllable consists of optional onset and coda slots, a simple or complex nucleus, one emic pitch or pitch cluster, and one mora of timing. [p. 77] ... 4.4.1 Vowel Length. audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage (sec. 5.4.2, p. 86) and all four supporting fragments (pp. 77, 81, 82) are verbatim at the stated locators in the WILC 9 PDF we hold; page image viewed directly. Deciding source: a 1991 SIL working-paper phonology by the fieldworkers, the only phonology Glottolog lists and the same source StressTyp2/WALS use; no reference grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study of Obokuitai exists in Glottolog's bibliography, and Clouse 1997 (downloaded now, Pacific Linguistics A-85 pp. 152, 160) defers to Jenison 1991 for tone and says stress is non-contrastive in all Lakes Plain languages, which is consistent with our reading that prominence is assigned by pitch height (highest pitch, rightmost on ties, final by default) rather than by quantity. sources.quote: p. 152: 'Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. ... Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991)'. p. 160: 'stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.'
sources.locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology', p. 152; Appendix 3 intro, p. 160
sources.note: Only other published work touching Obokuitai prosody; confirms the tone inventory (H, L, fall) after Jenison 1991 and states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain, supporting a caution that Obokuitai 'stress' is derivative of lexical pitch.
